newsitem.title: USA: Lykes ruling raises questions for APL-NOL merger.
newsitem.headline: Lykes ruling raises questions for APL-NOL merger.

text.p: The Maritime Administration's (Marad) rejection of operating subsidies for U.S. shipping company Lykes Bros has potentially serious implications for a merger between APL Ltd and Neptune Orient Lines Ltd, analysts said.
On Friday, Marad ruled that Lykes could not transfer more than $6.0 million in operating subsidies it stands to receive annually in light of its takeover by a foreign company, Canadian Pacific Ltd.
In its ruling, Marad said that Lykes' proposed transfer of the subsidies to CP would have resulted in "excessive foreign control" over U.S.-flag ships.
The subsidies are given to U.S. companies under the Maritime Security Program, which maintains U.S.-flagged ships with U.S. crews for military use during times of national emergency.

Although Marad stressed in its ruling that every case involving foreign participation in U.S.-flag companies is decided on its own merits, analysts said the decision reflected a wariness over foreign takeovers of U.S. shipping companies who participate in the maritime security fleet.
Standard & Poor's Stewart Scharf, who on Monday lowered its rating on APL shares to avoid from neutral, said the Marad ruling on Lykes could spell trouble for the APL-NOL link-up.

"This could negatively affect the (APL-NOL) merger," Scharf said. "With the U.S. government's showing signs of concern about shippers who receive subsidies being merged with foreign operators, there is a good likelihood that they could feel the same way about the APL-NOL merger."

In April, Singapore-based NOL announced its plan to acquire APL in a deal valued at about $825 million. Under the terms of the agreement, NOL will pay $33.50 per share for all 24.6 million outstanding shares of APL, the second-biggest shipping company in the U.S.
APL downplayed the impact of the Lykes ruling on its merger with NOL, saying it expected the deal to be wrapped up as scheduled in the fall.
"We intend to be able to fulfill all of Marad's requirements," said APL spokesman John Pachtner. "There were significant differences between our application and the Lykes application," he added.
At stake for APL are payments of $2.1 million a year for each of the nine U.S.-flagged vessels it operates within the Marad subsidy program.
APL said it expects to file "within a matter of days" its application with Marad to request continued receipt of subsidies following its merger with NOL.

The company has yet to reveal the details of its proposal to Marad, but Pachtner confirmed speculation that APL would comply with Marad's requirements by operating the U.S.-flagged ships under a U.S. company whose stock would be majority-held by U.S. citizens.
While APL clearly hopes to be able to remain in the maritime subsidy program, analysts said NOL is likely to proceed with its bid for APL regardless of how Marad rules.
Indeed, CP said on Monday it would forge ahead with its planned $34 million takeover of Lykes, which has been operating under Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection since October 1995.
"Is the (APL-NOL) deal predicated on getting those subsidies? I would say no," said Peter Shaerf, a maritime consultant in New York.
"Clearly it throws a huge warning sign onto the deal... but I think APL can walk away from the subsidies, too," he added.
